content: Viral infections are a major cause of illness and death in patients with hematological malignancies. However, it is unclear whether the use of viral vaccines in these patients is supported by strong evidence. To address this, researchers conducted a systematic review to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of viral vaccines in this population. The review included eight randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving a total of 593 patients, with 305 in the vaccine groups and 288 in the control groups. The studies assessed three types of vaccines: heat-inactivated varicella zoster virus (VZV) vaccine (two trials), inactivated influenza vaccines (five trials), and inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) (one trial). Seven of the trials were judged to have a high risk of bias, while one had a moderate risk of bias. The heat-inactivated VZV vaccine was evaluated for its ability to prevent herpes zoster (shingles). While the vaccine appeared to reduce the risk of herpes zoster compared to no vaccination (relative risk [RR] 0.54, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.3 to 1.0, P=0.05), the result was not statistically significant. However, one trial reported that the severity of herpes zoster was significantly lower in vaccinated patients compared to unvaccinated patients (mean difference [MD] 2.6, 95% CI 0.94 to 4.26, P=0.002). The vaccine also elicited an immune response but was associated with frequent local adverse effects, such as redness or swelling at the injection site. Inactivated influenza vaccines were studied in five trials. Two of these trials compared the vaccine to no vaccination and found that vaccinated patients had a significantly lower risk of developing lower respiratory tract infections (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.78, P=0.008) and a reduced risk of hospitalization (RR 0.17, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.31, P<0.00001). However, vaccine recipients were more likely to experience irritability and local adverse effects. One trial found no significant difference in seroconversion rates between patients who received one dose of the influenza vaccine and those who received two doses. Another trial found no difference in seroconversion between recombinant and standard influenza vaccines. Additionally, one study showed that administering the influenza vaccine with or without re-induction chemotherapy did not significantly affect seroconversion rates. The single trial evaluating the inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) compared vaccination initiated at 6 months versus 18 months after stem cell transplantation (SCT). This study found no significant difference in seroconversion rates between the two groups. In conclusion, the heat-inactivated VZV vaccine may reduce the severity of herpes zoster in adult stem cell transplant recipients, while the inactivated influenza vaccine may lower the risk of respiratory infections and hospitalization in adults with multiple myeloma or children with leukemia or lymphoma. However, the overall quality of evidence is low, and local adverse effects are common with these vaccines. Further high-quality RCTs are needed to provide more definitive evidence on the safety and efficacy of viral vaccines in patients with hematological malignancies.
